newsitem.title: UK: England, Wales power demand to break record again.
newsitem.headline: England, Wales power demand to break record again.

text.p: Electricity demand in England and Wales is expected to hit a new record on Wednesday evening, just 24 hours after it last did so, due to extremely cold weather, Rupert Corry of The National Grid Company Plc said.

Demand is expected to pass the 50,000 megawatt (MW) landmark at between 1700 and 1730 GMT on Wednesday, peaking at 50,030 MW and pipping by 300 MW the 49,730 MW record set on Tuesday at the same time.

"This winter's been quite remarkable," Corry said. "The last record dates from January last year but before that the last record was set in 1987. Yet suddenly we're seeing it break two days in a row."
He said the extra demand had been caused by the colder-than-normal weather.
Like much of Europe gripped in an Arctic chill, Britain has been hit by the coldest weather since the big freeze of 1963.

There is a small, steady growth in electricity consumption each year, he said, which may be explained partly by the growth in ownership of electrical appliances such as video recorders and microwave ovens.
But this has no discernible impact on peak demand except during cold weather.
The grid is confident of meeting demand. "There is enough to meet demand to maintain voltage and frequency on the system and all reserve requirements," Corry said.
Demand peaks in the winter between 1700 and 1730 GMT, the so-called "lighting up period", when industry is still running and domestic demand is starting.
It then falls away rapidly but there are regular evening peaks, known as "TV pick ups", on the hour and the half-hour.
This is related to people switching on electric kettles at the end of television programmes and, to a lesser extent, during advertisements.
There is also a small rise in demand at around 0100 GMT, Corry added, as electrical appliances such as night storage heaters working on cheap-rate electricity start to come on.
This lasts until between 0630 and 0730, depending on the pricing policy of the electricity generator, when they start to switch off, resulting in a decline in consumption.
Then early morning demand for water heating and breakfast kicks the day off again.
